939.title: The Ring of the Dove
939.hook: Ibn Hazm, jurist and poet, writes a book on love
939.howItsDone: The Ring of the Dove is read today as a classic of Arabic prose about love; readers often note that its author, Ibn Hazm, was also a jurist, and that the book closes with chapters on avoiding sin and practicing self-restraint.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ziryab, the singer from Baghdad who taught Cordoba new music and new meals. Your line was: music and manners. Did a recipe go to someone? Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

A man who writes on Islamic law, rigorous and famously sharp in argument, sits down to write about something else. A friend has asked him a question, the book's opening tells us: what is love, what are its signs, what happens to people inside it? He could have refused. Law books are serious, and this would be a book of glances, letters, messengers, jealousy, waiting at doors. He wrote it anyway, with poems of his own scattered through it. The writer was Ibn Hazm of Cordoba. The book is called The Ring of the Dove.
screen: `A JURIST GETS A QUESTION.` → `WHAT IS LOVE?` → `HE WRITES IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Ibn Hazm was a jurist who held to the plain, outward meaning of the Qur'an and the hadith, and he argued hard for it. That's what makes the book surprising. He doesn't treat love as a weakness to be scolded. He treats it as something to understand, the way he'd study any question. And he says early on that love in itself is not forbidden by religion or condemned by the law. What it leads to is a separate question. Then the book itself. It reads like a field guide. Chapters on the signs of love: the eyes that keep returning to one face, the conversation steered back to one name. On falling in love at a single look, and falling slowly over years. On keeping a secret, on the friend who carries messages, on faithfulness, on separation, on grief. He tells stories from his own life and from people he knew, honestly enough that some of them still sting. Where does love come from? Ibn Hazm leans toward the soul. He points to the Qur'an's account of humanity created from a single soul, with its mate made from it. Love, in his reading, has something to do with souls recognizing each other. The Qur'an itself says of spouses, in Pickthall's translation: "He ordained between you love and mercy." And then the ending, which is the jurist's signature. The last chapters turn to the ugliness of sin and the beauty of self-restraint. He doesn't pretend desire is tame. He just won't let the book end without asking what love is for. A man of rules, writing tenderly. A book on love.
screen: `A JURIST OF THE PLAIN MEANING.` · `A FIELD GUIDE TO LOVE'S SIGNS.` · `SOULS THAT RECOGNIZE EACH OTHER.` · `IT ENDS WITH SELF-RESTRAINT.` · then, large: `A BOOK ON LOVE.`

segments.voice: The practice: write to someone you love. Not yet, just get it ready. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind: a parent, a partner, a child, a friend you've drifted from. Notice one specific thing about them, the way Ibn Hazm notices: a habit, a phrase they always use, a moment you've never mentioned. Now find the first sentence you'd write to them. Keep it plain. Hold it until the bell. If you pray, you can remember this person in your prayer. If you don't, just keep their face in mind. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Hazm. The jurist of Cordoba who wrote The Ring of the Dove, a book on love and its signs, ending in self-restraint. Today's word.
Your line: a book on love. Today, send that first sentence to the person you thought of, on paper or by text, and let it be specific. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

940.title: Ibn Rushd
940.hook: the judge and philosopher of Cordoba, known in Europe as Averroes
940.howItsDone: Some students of philosophy and theology read Ibn Rushd's Decisive Treatise and his reply to al-Ghazali side by side with al-Ghazali's own work; Muslim scholars hold differing views on the place of philosophy in religious learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, The Ring of the Dove, Ibn Hazm's book on love, written by a jurist and ending in self-restraint. Your line was: a book on love. Did your first sentence reach the person you thought of? Day nine hundred forty.

Is it allowed, by the religious law itself, to study philosophy? Or is it required? That was the question a judge of Cordoba set out to answer in a short, tightly argued book. As a judge he ruled on inheritance and contracts. As a philosopher he wrote line-by-line commentaries on Aristotle, and those commentaries traveled north into Latin, where readers knew him by another name, Averroes. In Arabic he was Ibn Rushd, and he thought the Qur'an itself was sending people to think.
screen: `ALLOWED, OR REQUIRED?` → `A JUDGE WHO READ ARISTOTLE.` → `IN LATIN: AVERROES.`

segments.voice: The book is often called The Decisive Treatise, and it starts from the Qur'an, not from Aristotle. Ibn Rushd gathers verses that tell people to reflect. One of them ends, in Pickthall's translation: "So learn a lesson, O ye who have eyes!" Learn a lesson, reflect, cross over in your mind from what you see to what it means. If the Qur'an commands that, he argues, then those able to reason carefully about the world are being asked to do it, and the best tools for careful reasoning deserve to be learned, even from people outside the faith. He has a homely picture for this. If someone before you already made the knife for the sacrifice, you use the knife; you don't ask whether its maker shared your religion. You check that it cuts properly. Then the harder question: what if reasoning and scripture seem to clash? His answer: truth does not oppose truth. Where a proven conclusion meets the outward sense of a verse, the verse has a deeper reading that agrees with it, and the people trained to look should look. Not everyone agreed. Before him, the theologian al-Ghazali had written The Incoherence of the Philosophers, arguing that some of their conclusions went beyond what reason could prove and against what faith teaches. Ibn Rushd answered with a book called The Incoherence of the Incoherence. Muslims still read both of them, and still argue the question in both directions. What Ibn Rushd left on the table is a single conviction, worth saying slowly: the mind is not an intruder in the house of faith. Reason as a gift.
screen: `SO LEARN A LESSON, YE WHO HAVE EYES.` · `USE THE KNIFE THAT CUTS.` · `TRUTH DOES NOT OPPOSE TRUTH.` · `AL-GHAZALI DISAGREED.` · then, large: `REASON AS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one line of philosophy. Here's the one. Aristotle's Metaphysics, a book Ibn Rushd commented on, opens by saying that human beings, by nature, desire to know. Settle, and breathe. Turn that line over slowly. Is it true of you? What did you want to know today, even something small, like how a word is spelled or why the sky looked that color? Let one honest question rise and stay with it. If you pray, you can hold that question in your prayer. If you don't, just keep it in view. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Rushd. The judge of Cordoba, Averroes in Latin, who argued from the Qur'an that careful reasoning is a duty for those able to do it. Today's word.
Your line: reason as a gift. Today, take one question you'd normally shrug off and follow it for five minutes, to an answer or to a better question. Day nine hundred forty.

941.title: Ibn Arabi
941.hook: the mystic born in Murcia, who traveled east to Damascus
941.howItsDone: Some Sufi orders study Ibn Arabi's works closely and visit his tomb in Damascus; other Muslim scholars have criticized parts of his teaching, and the debate over him continues.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Rushd, the judge of Cordoba who argued that careful reasoning is a duty. Your line was: reason as a gift. Which question did you follow? Day nine hundred forty-one.

Yesterday's philosopher asks to meet a boy. The boy, in his own later telling, is barely grown, and people have been talking about him. Ibn Rushd rises to greet him and asks, more or less: is what you have found by inner opening the same as what we find by reasoning? The boy says yes. Ibn Rushd looks pleased. Then the boy says no. And between that yes and that no, the boy reports, the old philosopher went pale. The boy was Ibn Arabi, and the story is his own.

Ibn Arabi was born in Murcia, in al-Andalus, and never really stopped traveling. He went east, to Mecca, where he began a vast book called The Meccan Openings, and on through the cities of the Muslim world until he settled in Damascus, where he is buried. People called him al-Shaykh al-Akbar: the greatest master. What did he teach? Begin with a verse he and other Sufis return to. In Pickthall's translation: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." Ibn Arabi takes that line very seriously. In his reading, if God's face is wherever you turn, then the world is full of signs, and every moment can be a meeting. Elsewhere in the Qur'an, God says of each person, "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." For Ibn Arabi, knowing that nearness is not a conclusion you reason your way to. It is something opened in you, the inner opening behind his no to Ibn Rushd. Reason goes far, in his view, but there is a kind of knowing it can't hand you. Now the honest part. Ibn Arabi's books are dense and daring, and Muslims have read them in sharply different ways. Among his Sufi readers he is treasured. Some scholars, Ibn Taymiyya among them, attacked parts of his teaching as error. Others defended him as a master misunderstood. That argument is still going. So the title on today's carry comes with two words attached on purpose. The greatest master, some say.
screen: `FROM MURCIA TO DAMASCUS.` · `WHEREVER YOU TURN, GOD'S FACE.` · `A KNOWING THAT IS OPENED, NOT PROVED.` · `REVERED BY SOME, ATTACKED BY OTHERS.` · then, large: `THE GREATEST MASTER, SOME SAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit with one mystery. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing you can't explain and don't need to solve right now. Why you're here at all. Where a person you lost has gone. Why one moment last week felt so full. Don't argue with it, and don't try to crack it. Just let it sit beside you, the way Ibn Arabi let his yes and his no sit side by side. If your thoughts start building an answer, set the answer down gently and come back to the question. If you pray, you can bring the mystery into your prayer. If you don't, just keep it company. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Arabi. The mystic from Murcia who traveled to Damascus, called the greatest master by those who love him, and argued over by those who don't. Today's word.
Your line: the greatest master, some say. Today, when a question has two true answers, let yourself say yes and no, and see what opens between them. Day nine hundred forty-one.

942.title: Neighbors in al-Andalus
942.hook: Muslims, Jews and Christians shared cities and learning, alongside real tension and times of persecution
942.howItsDone: Muslims, Jews and Christians today remember al-Andalus in different ways; historians describe both its shared learning and its inequality and episodes of violence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Arabi, the mystic from Murcia who answered the philosopher yes, and then no. Your line was: the greatest master, some say. Did you let a question keep two answers? Day nine hundred forty-two.

A general sits in an army camp and writes a poem. In Hebrew. His name is Samuel ibn Naghrela. He is a Jew, he serves a Muslim king of Granada as vizier, the chief minister, and he leads that king's troops in the field. His Hebrew poems move in the meters of Arabic verse, and some were written on campaign: the night before a battle, the fear, the thanks for coming home alive. A Jewish commander, a Muslim court, Hebrew words in Arabic rhythms. That is one face of al-Andalus. Keep his family's name in mind, because his son's story shows the other face, and today needs both.
screen: `A JEWISH VIZIER WRITES A POEM.` → `HEBREW IN ARABIC METERS.` → `HIS SON'S STORY IS THE OTHER FACE.`

segments.voice: Start with the frame. The Qur'an calls Jews and Christians People of the Book, and under Muslim rule in al-Andalus they lived as protected communities. They kept their own worship, their own clergy, their own courts. They also paid a special tax and lived under limits a Muslim neighbor didn't. Protection and inequality, in the same arrangement. Now the sharing. At the court of Abd al-Rahman the Third, a Jewish physician named Hasdai ibn Shaprut served as a trusted diplomat. Jewish poets, Samuel among them, wrote Hebrew verse in the patterns of Arabic poetry. Philosophers of all three communities argued over the same Greek books, read in Arabic. And now the other side, said just as plainly. In Cordoba, some Christians who publicly denounced Islam were executed, and their community remembered them as martyrs. In Granada, a mob turned on the Jews of the city, and among the dead was the vizier Joseph, Samuel's own son. Later, under the Almohad rulers, Jews and Christians faced pressure to convert, and some fled; the family of the Jewish scholar Maimonides was among those who left. Christian kingdoms to the north, meanwhile, were pushing south by war. So which was it, harmony or persecution? The honest answer is both, at different times, in different cities, under different rulers. The Qur'an gives a reason for difference, in Pickthall's words: "We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Knowing one another includes knowing the hard chapters. Shared, and not simple.
screen: `PROTECTED, AND NOT EQUAL.` · `A JEWISH DIPLOMAT, ARABIC METERS.` · `MARTYRS, A MOB, A FAMILY THAT FLED.` · `THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.` · then, large: `SHARED, AND NOT SIMPLE.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to learn about your neighbors' history. Settle, and breathe. Think of a neighbor, a coworker, a classmate, someone whose family comes from a story different from yours. What do you actually know about where they come from? Let one honest question form: how did their people come to be here, what did they carry, what did they lose? Hold that question gently. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer. If you don't, just hold them in mind with good will. The bell holds the time.
Neighbors in al-Andalus. Muslims, Christians and Jews sharing cities, words and books, alongside inequality, tension and times of persecution. Today's word.
Your line: shared, and not simple. Today, look up one thing about the history of a community near you that isn't your own, and read past the first easy summary. Day nine hundred forty-two.

943.title: The Alhambra
943.hook: the red palace of Granada, walls covered with the words, no victor but Allah
943.howItsDone: Visitors to the Alhambra, Muslim and not, read the motto 'no victor but God' carved throughout its walls; Muslims often say that victory comes only from God, echoing the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday, neighbors in al-Andalus: Muslims, Christians and Jews sharing cities and words, alongside inequality and violence. Your line was: shared, and not simple. What did you learn past the easy summary? Day nine hundred forty-three.

Stand in a courtyard in Granada and look closely at the wall. What looks like lace from a few steps back turns out, up close, to be writing. Arabic letters, carved into plaster, woven through vines and stars. Some of it is the Qur'an. Some is poetry, praising the very room you're standing in. And again and again, one short sentence, small enough to fit in a corner and patient enough to fill a palace. Wa la ghaliba illa Allah. There is no victor but God. Today: the Alhambra.
screen: `LACE THAT TURNS OUT TO BE WRITING.` → `QUR'AN, POETRY, AND ONE SENTENCE.` → `NO VICTOR BUT GOD.`

segments.voice: The Alhambra sits on a hill above Granada. Its name is said to mean the red one, for the color of its walls. It was the palace of the Nasrid rulers of Granada. By then their map had shrunk: the Christian kingdoms had taken city after city, and Granada was what remained. That makes the motto on the walls worth hearing twice. There's a story people tell about it. The dynasty's founder came home from a battle, and the crowd hailed him as the victor. His answer, so the story goes, was the sentence that would cover his family's palace: no victor but God. Nobody can confirm the scene, but the sentence is carved there for anyone to read. It isn't a verse of the Qur'an word for word, but it leans on one. In Pickthall's translation, the Qur'an says: "Victory cometh only from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise." A ruler writing that on his own walls is saying something odd for a ruler. The win is not mine. The throne answers to someone else. Then there's the craft. The writing doesn't sit on top of the decoration; it is the decoration. Letters climb, interlace, turn into borders. Geometry repeats without ending. The poems on some walls speak in the room's own voice, as if the building were talking. A palace, in other words, that keeps reminding its owners who owns it. And a sentence modest enough to carry anywhere. No victor but Allah.
screen: `THE RED PALACE ON THE HILL.` · `A STORY ABOUT A VICTORY.` · `VICTORY COMETH ONLY FROM ALLAH.` · `THE WRITING IS THE DECORATION.` · then, large: `NO VICTOR BUT ALLAH.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at its calligraphy, first in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture a wall where a single sentence is carved over and over, among leaves and stars, until your eye stops seeing the pattern and starts reading it. Now bring to mind one thing you've won lately: a deadline met, an argument settled, a good day. Hold it lightly, and let the sentence sit beside it. No victor but God. If you pray, you can let those words rest on your breath. If you don't, simply notice how it feels to hold a win more loosely. The bell holds the time.
The Alhambra. The red palace of Granada, where Qur'an, poetry and one motto are carved into the walls: no victor but God. Today's word.

Your line: no victor but allah. Today, look up one photograph of the Alhambra's carved walls, and the next time you win something, small or large, notice who and what helped it happen. If you pray, you can say the line. Day nine hundred forty-three.

944.title: 1492 and after
944.hook: Granada falls, and the Muslims of Spain are later forced to convert or leave
944.howItsDone: The loss of al-Andalus and the expulsion of the Moriscos are remembered in Muslim histories, poetry and sermons; some families in North Africa trace their roots to the Moriscos.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Alhambra, the red palace whose walls repeat one sentence. Your line was: no victor but allah. After a win, who and what did you notice helping? Day nine hundred forty-four.

South of Granada there's a mountain pass with a name that is really a story: the sigh of the Moor. People tell that the sultan who handed Granada over, Abu Abdallah, whom the Spanish called Boabdil, rode out with his household, stopped at that pass, turned for one last look at the city and the red palace, and wept. Whether he wept there, nobody can say for certain. What came after his surrender is better documented, and it is harder to hear. Today: fourteen ninety-two, and after.
screen: `THE SIGH OF THE MOOR.` → `ONE LAST LOOK BACK.` → `WHAT CAME AFTER.`

segments.voice: Granada did not fall in a final battle. It was surrendered by treaty to Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic monarchs of Spain, and the treaty made promises. Muslims could keep their mosques, their faith, their law, their property. Those promises did not last. Before long the authorities were pressing Muslims to be baptized, and in time, across Spain, the choice became baptism or exile. Families who stayed, because home was home, were baptized, and they came to be called Moriscos. Some of them became sincere Christians. Others kept Islam in secret, praying behind closed doors, teaching children quietly. And they wrote. Some Moriscos wrote Spanish in Arabic letters, copying prayers, stories of the prophets, and rules of worship in a script their neighbors couldn't read. A language hiding inside another language, so that faith could survive in a kitchen. The suspicion never lifted. There were rebellions, crushed. And in the end the Moriscos as a whole, even those who were truly Christian, were expelled from Spain, crossing to North Africa and beyond. Their neighbors had been through it already. In the same year Granada surrendered, the Jews of Spain were ordered to convert or leave, and Jewish families left. Two communities, the same choice. This closes our walk through al-Andalus, and this ending belongs in the story too, beside the arches and the books. Remember the Moriscos.
screen: `SURRENDERED, WITH PROMISES.` · `BAPTISM OR EXILE.` · `SPANISH IN ARABIC LETTERS.` · `EXPELLED, AS THE JEWS HAD BEEN.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE MORISCOS.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for the displaced, or if you don't pray, hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of a family made to leave a home they loved, the Moriscos at a harbor, or people forced from their homes today, whose names you may have heard in the news. Picture one ordinary thing they had to leave behind: a door key, a kitchen, a tree in a yard. Stay with that one thing. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer, in whatever words are already yours. If you don't, just keep them company in your attention. The bell holds the time.
Moriscos. The Muslims who stayed in Spain after Granada surrendered in fourteen ninety-two, forced to convert and, in the end, expelled. Today's word.
Your line: remember the moriscos. Today, learn the story of one group of people displaced from their home, past or present, and say their name aloud once. Day nine hundred forty-four.

945.title: Fatimah al-Fihri's Qarawiyyin
945.hook: a woman in Fez spends her inheritance on a mosque that becomes a place of learning
945.howItsDone: The Qarawiyyin in Fez is still a working mosque and a center of Islamic learning, and Muslims often cite Fatimah al-Fihri as an example of charity that keeps giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fourteen ninety-two and after: Granada surrendered, promises broke, and the Moriscos were forced to convert and then expelled. Your line was: remember the moriscos. Whose name did you say aloud? Day nine hundred forty-five.

An inheritance arrives. A father has died, and his daughter now has money of her own. What do you do with it? A house, a business, a cushion for bad years. In Fez, in Morocco, a woman named Fatimah al-Fihri, whose family had come to the city from Kairouan, the chronicle says, chose a mosque. It would become the Qarawiyyin, and it would not stay only a mosque. Today we cross the strait to North Africa.
screen: `AN INHERITANCE ARRIVES.` → `SHE CHOOSES A MOSQUE.` → `IT WON'T STAY ONLY A MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Much of the story comes from a later chronicle of Fez, which tells it simply. Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad al-Fihri, was a devout woman. She spent what she inherited on building the mosque, from the ground up. Tradition adds a detail: that she fasted through the whole time the building went on. And the chronicle says her sister Maryam did the same thing across the river, building a mosque for the other half of the city. Two sisters, two inheritances, two mosques. Why would someone do this? There's a hadith that fits her story. Sahih Muslim records the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in substance: when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except for three things. Charity that keeps flowing. Knowledge that people go on benefiting from. A good child who prays for them. Fatimah's mosque turned out to be the first two at once. Prayer filled it, and then teaching did. Scholars gathered there to teach the Qur'an, law, grammar, and later much more, and students came from far away to sit in its circles. Over time it grew into what Fez now calls the University of al-Qarawiyyin. So the carry is not an exaggeration, just a long view: she built a mosque, and a university grew in it. Look back over this week, and it's full of builders: a jurist who wrote on love, a judge who defended reason, a mystic, neighbors who built a shared culture and a fragile one, a palace that credited God with every win, a people who kept faith in hiding. And now a daughter with an inheritance. She founded a university.
screen: `A DAUGHTER'S INHERITANCE.` · `TWO SISTERS, TWO MOSQUES.` · `CHARITY THAT KEEPS FLOWING.` · `FROM PRAYER HALL TO UNIVERSITY.` · then, large: `SHE FOUNDED A UNIVERSITY.`

segments.voice: The practice: honor a woman who founded something. Settle, and breathe. Bring one woman to mind who started something that outlasted the moment. A grandmother who began a family tradition. A teacher who started a reading club. A neighbor who organized the food drive. Someone famous, or someone only you know about. Picture what she built, and who is still benefiting from it. Let gratitude for her sit with you. If you pray, you can remember her in your prayer. If you don't, simply hold her name with thanks.
